analysis.one_liner: Makes the Bush-era tax cuts permanent, repeals the estate tax and AMT, and cuts the corporate rate to 25%.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote, a hearing, or any action after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make permanent the income tax rate cuts from 2001 and 2003, including the low rates on capital gains and dividends. It would permanently repeal the estate and gift tax, repeal the individual alternative minimum tax, and cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25%. The bill never moved after being referred to the tax-writing committee; no hearing, no vote, and the 112th Congress ended with it still sitting in committee.
analysis.who_benefits: High earners, heirs to large estates, and corporations gain the most. The estate tax repeal and AMT repeal are aimed at wealthier households, and the corporate rate cut goes to shareholders and profitable companies. Middle-income filers also keep the 2001-2003 rate cuts, but those gains are smaller in dollar terms than what flows to the top.

how_it_helps.text: Makes permanent the reduced income tax rates from the 2001 and 2003 tax laws, including the lower rates on dividends and capital gains, which would otherwise have been scheduled to change at the end of 2012.
Permanently repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for estates of decedents dying after 2010, so large inheritances would pass free of federal estate tax.
Repeals the alternative minimum tax on individual taxpayers, which falls mainly on higher-income households with certain deductions.
Cuts the maximum corporate income tax rate from 35% to 25%, including for personal service corporations.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue falls, and the shortfall would be made up by more borrowing or future spending cuts. The gains concentrate among the top: the estate tax repeal benefits only the largest estates, and lower rates on capital gains and dividends are claimed disproportionately by high-income filers.

drawbacks.text: Making the tax cuts permanent without any offset reduces federal revenue permanently, enlarging deficits that fall on future taxpayers.
The largest dollar benefits go to the highest earners: the estate tax repeal affects only the largest estates, and capital gains and dividend income is concentrated among high-income households.
Repealing the alternative minimum tax eliminates a backstop that limited how much high earners could lower their taxes through deductions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The rate cuts reach middle-income families too, so the benefit is real but uneven; the estate tax repeal and AMT repeal are aimed almost entirely at the top, and the bill offers nothing to cover the lost revenue, so the cost lands on future taxpayers through larger deficits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it never reached the House floor and the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michele Bachmann introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the first week of the new Congress, with Reps. Steve King and Bobby Schilling as original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Six Republicans cosponsored the bill, all from the same party.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the federal government avoided the permanent revenue loss from the tax cuts, and the estate tax and AMT remained in place as they would have otherwise.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers who kept the estate tax

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors and the sponsor were Republicans, and no Democrat backed the bill; it never advanced far enough to produce a roll call.

industries.note: The estate tax repeal, AMT repeal, and permanent low rates on capital gains and dividends deliver the largest dollar savings to the wealthiest families. The cost shows up as lost federal revenue that everyone else shares.
Cutting the top corporate rate from 35% to 25% raises after-tax profits for profitable companies. The revenue loss is borne by general taxpayers.

Middle-income filers would have kept the lower rates from the 2001 and 2003 tax laws. That benefit is real but smaller in dollars than what the bill gives the top, and it comes without any way to pay for it.
